Determine whether training can improve low-rank compressibility while preserving model quality.

sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

inspect:2610.11730.question: What were the matched-validation-loss controls, standard weight-decay and compression baselines, compression metrics, and label-noise experimental controls for spectral weight decay?

passages.text: BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

• We formulate spectral weight decay as decoupled nuclear-norm regularization, derive its additive singular-value shrinkage, and connect the update to approximate proximal descent. • Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay improves low-rank compression and inference speed over standard weight decay at matched validation loss. It also outperforms Cuttlefish and Prehab in matched compression comparisons. • On image and text classification tasks, spectral weight decay improves fixed-horizon robustness to label noise over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization.

Spectral weight decay lowers the effective rank of weight matrices, making them amenable to low-rank compression. We use SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] , which gives the lowest validation loss in our matched comparison. We compress each weight matrix to its own effective rank, which varies substantially across layers (Figure 2 , middle). We leave the token embeddings and output head uncompressed because their ranks respond little to spectral weight decay, and compressing them even to their effective ranks sharply degrades model quality. The comparison and compression procedure are described in Appendix B.4 . Figure 3 (top) reports the maximum compression rate supported by each validation-loss distortion budget. Spectral weight decay substantially shifts this frontier upward at all three model scales. For the 500 500 M model and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it supports 1.89 × 1.89\times compression, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times after standard weight decay. The same factorization reduces the FLOPs of a linear layer when r ⁡ ( m + n ) < m ​ n r(m+n)<mn . This reduction does not translate directly into lower latency because the factorized forward pass evaluates ( U r ​ Σ r ) ​ ( V r ⊤ ​ X ) (U_{r}\Sigma_{r})(V_{r}^{\top}X) with two GEMMs instead of the single GEMM W ​ X WX . The additional kernel launch and intermediate activation can offset the reduction in FLOPs. To improve tensor-core utilization, we round the effective rank down to the nearest multiple of 16 16 , r l = max ⁡ ( 16 , 16 ​ ⌊ erank ⁡ ( W l ) 16 ⌋ ) , r_{l}=\max\!\left(16,\,16\left\lfloor\frac{\operatorname{erank}(W_{l})}{16}\right\rfloor\right), (3)

Adjusting an aligned rank by one step, ± 16 \pm 16 , has negligible effect on validation loss. We therefore use this rank-aligned compression scheme throughout. The factorized models outperform their dense counterparts only at large batch sizes, so we measure forward-pass latency with a batch size of 256 256 on a single GPU. For the 500 500 M model, spectral weight decay yields a 1.09 × 1.09\times speedup near a 2 % 2\% distortion budget and reaches 1.18 × 1.18\times at 4 % 4\% , compared with 1.01 × 1.01\times under standard weight decay (Figure 3 , bottom).

passages.text: Monarch–Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining Alexander Miasnikov 1 , Kabirov Ruslan 1 , Gleb Molodtsov 1 , Dmitrii Vlashchuk 1 , Vladimir Aletov 1 , Nail Bashirov 1 , Daniil Tikhonov 1,2 , Maxim Krutikov 1 , Aleksandr Shestakov 1,3,* , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1 1 BRAIn Lab 2 HSE University 3 MBZUAI * Work performed at BRAIn Lab prior to joining MBZUAI. Code: https://github.com/brain-lab-research/monarch-muon Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch–Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch–Muon improves over Monarch–AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch–Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

Table 1 : Pretraining on FineWeb-Edu under a common training recipe within each architecture. Optimizer Val. loss Active params Total params Dense 257M AdamW 3.02 257M 257M Muon 2.99 257M 257M GaLore 3.07 257M 257M Monarch–AdamW, 2 blocks 3.09 224M 224M Monarch–Muon, 2 blocks 3.06 224M 224M Monarch–AdamW, 4 blocks 3.16 164M 164M Monarch–Muon, 4 blocks 3.14 164M 164M MoE AdamW 2.68 280M 1.029B Muon 2.65 280M 1.029B Monarch–AdamW, 2 blocks 2.77 237M 767M Monarch–Muon, 2 blocks 2.68 237M 767M Monarch–AdamW, 4 blocks 2.79 171M 436M Monarch–Muon, 4 blocks 2.75 171M 436M We evaluate Monarch–Muon through four comparisons: optimization quality at fixed Monarch structure, training costs as model width increases, initialization for dense-to-Monarch transfer, and compatibility with FP8. Quality runs train a 257M dense reference and a 1B MoE reference on FineWeb-Edu ( Penedo et al., 2024 ) . Systems benchmarks cover dense reference sizes up to 6.89B on an H100. These benchmarks measure the cost of the training operations at larger widths, while the complete pretraining runs test learning quality. Appendix A gives the protocols.

Structure reduces more than the optimizer state: it also compresses the trainable weights and gradients. For Muon, the smaller blocks additionally reduce the cost of orthogonalization. Section 3.2 derives the distinct scaling laws: square-factor storage decreases as 2 / m 2/m of the dense matrix, while Newton–Schulz arithmetic decreases as 2 / m 2 2/m^{2} , where m m is the block count. We test how these savings translate to allocated memory and wall time across five dense reference sizes, using four-block Monarch models and a common microbatch of four. Table 2 includes both optimizer and full-step measurements. Timings for projection-based methods exclude their periodic projection refreshes. The benefit grows with width because cheaper orthogonalization is increasingly accompanied by cheaper forward and backward passes. inspect:2610.04249.question: What balance and singular-vector alignment assumptions underpin the optimizer comparisons, and what experiments test the predicted low-rank bias on Transformers or language models versus matrix factorization?

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Figure 1: Optimizer geometry sets the pace of spectral learning. In balanced aligned deep matrix factorization, GD and Muon produce distinct spectral learning trajectories (experimental details in App. F ). (a) Under GD, larger target modes are learned earlier, while smaller modes remain suppressed for longer. (b) Under Muon, factor amplitudes grow at a common speed, allowing smaller targets to reach full recovery earlier. (c) From the same initial amplitude 0.01 0.01 , Muon accelerates the growth of a positive target mode (red) and, importantly, removes the zero target mode in finite time (blue). GD instead exhibits delayed growth and slow decay. Thus, faster emergence of weak modes does not imply weaker removal of unsupported modes. Optimizer geometry determines which spectral components emerge, persist, and disappear. Other optimizers are discussed in later sections.

Our approach separates the geometry induced by the factorization from the update rule and state maintained by the optimizer. The product dynamics first express how each layer updates combine into the dynamics of the effective matrix. Under explicit balance, target alignment, and state compatibility assumptions, this description reduces to a common equation for each singular mode. The factorization determines how factor dynamics changes the mode amplitude, while the optimizer determines the update through its normalization, accumulated statistics, and damping. This gives a controlled setting in which these mechanisms can be compared without attributing differences to changing singular directions. Our analysis separates three aspects of spectral learning that are often conflated: the birth of initially small nonzero modes to reach a prescribed amplitude, saturation near their targets, and decay of unsupported modes whose target is zero. These phases need not respond to an optimizer in the same way. A method can permit rapid emergence while retaining a slow decay tail, and accumulated gradient history can change the rate at which an already learned component settles. Consequently, the emergence of small modes alone does not describe the spectral bias of an entire trajectory as studied in prior works. Our results make these distinctions explicit as shown in Fig. 1 . Moreover, it also brings out how optimizer state parameters, including adaptive stabilization and curvature damping, interpolate between distinct rank selection regimes, and verifies that these differences persist in underdetermined matrix factorization and regression. Our contributions are: ( 𝟏 ) \mathbf{(1)} A common framework for spectral learning. We express effective matrix dynamics through the layer

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

Our analysis shows that the spectral bias of depth depends on optimizer geometry and the stage of training. A surprising consequence is that rapid learning of weak components can coexist with rapid removal of unsupported ones, as illustrated by the Muon analysis. Conversely, accumulated history can accelerate the emergence of a mode while prolonging its persistence. These effects make a single ordering of optimizers by stronger or weaker low-rank bias inadequate. A further implication is that parameters associated with numerical stability also shape learning bias. In the analyzed models, Adam’s stabilizer, Shampoo’s accumulator initialization, and K-FAC’s damping determine where normalization, history, or curvature correction governs spectral progress. They can therefore change how strongly depth suppresses small modes, even within the same optimizer. Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior. This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

passages.section: Low-rank bias and the limits of norm descriptions.
passages.text: Gunasekar et al. (2017) investigate implicit regularization in two-layer matrix factorization and conjecture a nuclear-norm characterization in a restricted commuting setting. Arora et al. (2019) extend the analysis to depth and derive singular-value-dependent mobility under balanced gradient flow, showing that depth strengthens the tendency toward low-rank solutions. Razin and Cohen (2020) construct matrix-completion problems in which norms diverge as the loss vanishes, demonstrating the limits of a universal norm-minimization account. Li et al. (2021) instead develop a greedy low-rank learning interpretation under explicit assumptions. A complementary trajectory perspective is provided by Neural Tangent Kernel and lazy-training analyses, which characterize sufficiently wide networks through a linearization around initialization and an approximately fixed kernel governing function-space evolution ( Jacot et al., 2018 ; Lee et al., 2019 ; Sabanayagam et al., 2022 ) . In contrast, our analysis retains the nonlinear multiplicative parameterization and its evolving, optimizer-dependent spectral mobility, allowing us to compare the birth, saturation, and decay of singular modes before convergence.

Our results make these distinctions explicit as shown in Fig. 1 . Moreover, it also brings out how optimizer state parameters, including adaptive stabilization and curvature damping, interpolate between distinct rank selection regimes, and verifies that these differences persist in underdetermined matrix factorization and regression. Our contributions are: ( 𝟏 ) \mathbf{(1)} A common framework for spectral learning. We express effective matrix dynamics through the layer

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

Our analysis shows that the spectral bias of depth depends on optimizer geometry and the stage of training. A surprising consequence is that rapid learning of weak components can coexist with rapid removal of unsupported ones, as illustrated by the Muon analysis. Conversely, accumulated history can accelerate the emergence of a mode while prolonging its persistence. These effects make a single ordering of optimizers by stronger or weaker low-rank bias inadequate. A further implication is that parameters associated with numerical stability also shape learning bias. In the analyzed models, Adam’s stabilizer, Shampoo’s accumulator initialization, and K-FAC’s damping determine where normalization, history, or curvature correction governs spectral progress. They can therefore change how strongly depth suppresses small modes, even within the same optimizer. Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior. This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

Gunasekar et al. (2017) investigate implicit regularization in two-layer matrix factorization and conjecture a nuclear-norm characterization in a restricted commuting setting. Arora et al. (2019) extend the analysis to depth and derive singular-value-dependent mobility under balanced gradient flow, showing that depth strengthens the tendency toward low-rank solutions. inspect:2611.07859.question: In the controlled closed-search experiments, how were CORE and the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses matched for corpus, retriever, agent model, tool budget, and returned context length? What answer-accuracy, evidence-recall, and token-cost results and limitations are reported?

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. Under controlled settings, we compare CORE with two recent state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, Tongyi DeepResearch ( Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2025 ) and OpenResearcher ( Li et al., 2026b ) , on BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , BrowseComp-Wikipedia ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus CM ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) . To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

We compare CORE with existing deep research harnesses on three benchmarks, and a component analysis examines the contributions of coarse-to-fine search and context management. We find that Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B, using the original Tongyi DeepResearch harness with document-level retrieval based on AgentIR-4B, achieves 63.13% on BrowseComp-Plus, which is lower than the 65.66% achieved by our current passage-level retrieval setup. On BrowseComp-Plus, Jiang et al. (2026) report an evidence recall of 38.1% for Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B, whereas their Harness-1 (20B) reported the evidence recall at 58.4%.

We presented CORE , a training-free deep research harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves whole passages to judge relevance, then reuses the reranker’s token-level similarities to return only the most relevant snippet from each one. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. Across three agent models and three benchmarks, CORE achieves higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher in every model–benchmark comparison, while returning substantially fewer tokens per search than Tongyi DeepResearch. These results show that deep research agents can answer more accurately from shorter search responses when relevant text is selected before it enters their context.

Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

inspect:2610.06116.question: In the LLaMA and Qwen3 pretraining experiments, how are ORCA and Muon matched for tokens, compute, hyperparameter tuning, and architecture? What measured effective-rank, validation-loss, compressibility, and runtime results support or limit the claimed benefit of temporary orthogonality regularization?

passages.text: Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. We introduce ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After), a minimal optimizer intervention that applies strong but temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in training, then removes it. This allows the weights to benefit from a broader spectrum early on and adapt freely afterward. Across LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained mixture-of-experts models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon. Its loss reduction relative to Muon matches or exceeds Muon’s reduction relative to Adam. Ablations support the early-shaping, later-release design. Further, ORCA requires no architectural changes and adds minimal overhead. An implementation is available at https://github.com/uuurraaa/ORCA_Optimizer .

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

The advantage of ORCA holds over a wide range of learning rates: at every learning rate evaluated for both methods, ORCA reaches a lower final validation loss than Muon, and at all evaluated configurations between 10 − 3 10^{-3} and 5 × 10 − 3 5\times 10^{-3} it is even better than fully tuned Muon. The independent searches select 1.3 × 10 − 3 1.3\times 10^{-3} , 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , 10 − 3 10^{-3} , and 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} for Adam, Muon, Pion, and ORCA, with final validation losses of 2.8824 2.8824 , 2.8460 2.8460 , 2.9790 2.9790 , and 2.8106 2.8106 , respectively; ORCA thus lowers the loss by a further 0.0354 0.0354 relative to the best Muon and stays within 0.002 0.002 of its own optimum across 1.6 × 10 − 3 1.6\times 10^{-3} to 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , showing that the improvement does not rely on a narrow learning-rate choice. LLama Pretraining Tasks. We compare ORCA against Adam and Muon on LLaMA 350M and 1.3B, training each model for 100B tokens. As shown in Figure 4.1 , Muon outperforms Adam at both scales, while ORCA further lowers the validation loss. Compared with Muon, ORCA reduces the final loss by 0.0194 0.0194 at 350M and 0.0244 0.0244 at 1.3B, with consistent gains at both scales. Further, a four-seed robustness result for the 130M, 50k-step setting is reported in Appendix C . We also evaluate the final ORCA and Muon LLaMA 1.3B checkpoints from Figure 4.1 on five downstream tasks ( Clark et al., 2018 ; Zellers et al., 2019 ; Sakaguchi et al., 2021 ; Bisk et al., 2020 ) . As shown in Table 4.1 , ORCA outperforms Muon on all five tasks. This suggests that the lower pre-training loss of ORCA also leads to better downstream performance.

We also evaluate how the optimization performance translates into token efficiency by measuring the training required to reach a common target loss. We continued ORCA from its original 51k-step checkpoint, starting the final decay early, and reached a validation loss of 2.318 at approximately 60k steps. The standard Muon run, using its original 100k-step settings, reached the same loss at 100k steps ( Figure 2(a) ). Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain. To save compute, we reused the checkpoint without retuning ORCA for the shorter run: its original 25k-step shaping stage accounts for 41.7% of the 60k-step budget rather than the tuned default of 25%. The 8 8 B experiment extends this result to a larger model trained on 100 100 B tokens, where ORCA also finishes below Muon ( Figure 4.4 ). Across these MoE experiments, ORCA reduces final validation loss by 0.020 0.020 – 0.025 0.025 relative to Muon.

These results show that the benefits of early orthogonal shaping extend beyond Muon to other base optimizers. inspect:2610.08049.question: What language-model fine-tuning tasks and backbones test the proposed Riemannian LoRA metric, and how does it compare with standard LoRA and other preconditioned LoRA methods at matched rank, training budget, and optimizer settings? Report measured quality and training-memory or runtime costs.

passages.text: LoRA was initially formulated by Hu et al. [21] and achieves comparable full fine-tuning performance despite having very few trainable parameters. However, it often exhibits a performance gap compared to full fine-tuning. We here summarize several studies to improve the performance of LoRA. Modeling (Architecture). Beyond the standard two-factor factorization [ 21 , 41 , 36 , 24 ] as described in 2 , three-factor factorization has been proposed recently [ 58 , 26 , 41 ] , which inserts a small trainable matrix between B B and A A to fuse more information and flexibly. Other approaches have also been explored, such as adapting low-rank values at each module [ 66 ] , incorporating the mixture-of-experts architecture [ 15 , 32 , 16 , 50 ] , exploiting multiple LoRA modules [ 59 , 28 , 30 ] , and introducing non-linear mapping [ 13 ] . In this paper, we adopt the standard two-factor modeling 2 as a first step and leave the expansion for other advanced modelings to future work.

Initialization. Hu et al. [21] originally proposed to use a random Gaussian initialization for A A and set zero for B B to ensure that B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} is zero at the beginning of training. Later, several initialization strategies have proposed to utilize the pre-trained weight characteristics [ 33 , 54 ] . These methods differ in how they initialize B B and A A , using the largest singular values and corresponding vectors of the pre-trained weight matrix [ 33 ] or smaller ones [ 54 ] . On the other hand, Wang et al. [55] and Zhang et al. [67] initialized B B and A A using the singular values and corresponding vectors of the one-step gradient of full fine-tuning. In this paper, we follow the standard initialization proposed in [ 21 ] and the combination with the advanced initialization strategies is left for future work.

Optimization. Several optimization approaches for LoRA have been proposed [ 56 , 69 , 26 , 41 ] . For example, Wang et al. [56] aligned the gradient of LoRA with that of full fine-tuning by solving a minimization problem for this gap 2 2 2 We further discuss the relationship between this method and our method in Appendix E . . To fully exploit low-dimensional subspaces spanned by the columns of B B and A A , Zhu et al. [69] regularized those subspaces to capture complementary information. Along this, Li et al. [26] and Park et al. [41] exploited the geometry of Stiefel manifold that imposes the orthogonal constraints on B B and/or A A . On the other hand, exploiting the invariance of LoRA has been studied [ 63 , 50 ] . As explained in Sec. 1 , this approach induces preconditioning at each gradient step described in 4 and achieves efficient optimization compared to the original LoRA. This approach is the first Riemannian preconditioning study for LoRA, and its underlying idea is inspired by the classical low-rank matrix completion problem [ 36 ] . Note that, in the literature on low-rank matrix (or tensor) completion problem, several preconditioning variants have been proposed [ 51 , 65 , 64 ] . Our work follows the Riemannian preconditioning for LoRA proposed in [ 63 , 50 ] but designs a Riemannian metric tailored to LoRA for more efficient optimization.

Following [ 21 , 63 ] , we conducted LoRA fine-tuning for the GPT-2 medium model [ 45 ] on E2E natural language generation challenge task [ 38 ] , which assesses the fine-tuned model’s ability to generate fluent and semantically accurate sentences from meaning representations. We followed the same experimental setup as in [ 63 ] , except that we tuned the learning rate over { 0.02 , 0.04 , … , 0.30 } \{0.02,0.04,\dots,0.30\} for SGD and { 0.0002 , 0.0004 , … , 0.0030 } \{0.0002,0.0004,\dots,0.0030\} for AdamW methods on the validation set. For all methods, we inserted the low-rank matrix B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} into the query and value matrices of the attention layers in the GPT-2 model. We also fixed the rank to r = 4 r=4 , the scaling factor of B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} to 32 32 , the batch size to 8 8 , the dropout to 0.1 0.1 , and the train epoch to 5 5 with a linear learning-rate schedule. We set the weight decay to 0.01 0.01 for the SGD and AdamW methods. We evaluated all methods by five metrics, BLEU [ 40 ] , NIST [ 12 ] , METEOR [ 3 ] , ROUGE-L [ 27 ] , and CIDEr [ 53 ] , on the test set. LoRA was initially formulated by Hu et al. [21] and achieves comparable full fine-tuning performance despite having very few trainable parameters. However, it often exhibits a performance gap compared to full fine-tuning. We here summarize several studies to improve the performance of LoRA. Modeling (Architecture). Beyond the standard two-factor factorization [ 21 , 41 , 36 , 24 ] as described in 2 , three-factor factorization has been proposed recently [ 58 , 26 , 41 ] , which inserts a small trainable matrix between B B and A A to fuse more information and flexibly. Other approaches have also been explored, such as adapting low-rank values at each module [ 66 ] , incorporating the mixture-of-experts architecture [ 15 , 32 , 16 , 50 ] , exploiting multiple LoRA modules [ 59 , 28 , 30 ] , and introducing non-linear mapping [ 13 ] . In this paper, we adopt the standard two-factor modeling 2 as a first step and leave the expansion for other advanced modelings to future work.

Initialization. Hu et al. [21] originally proposed to use a random Gaussian initialization for A A and set zero for B B to ensure that B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} is zero at the beginning of training. Later, several initialization strategies have proposed to utilize the pre-trained weight characteristics [ 33 , 54 ] . These methods differ in how they initialize B B and A A , using the largest singular values and corresponding vectors of the pre-trained weight matrix [ 33 ] or smaller ones [ 54 ] . On the other hand, Wang et al. [55] and Zhang et al. [67] initialized B B and A A using the singular values and corresponding vectors of the one-step gradient of full fine-tuning. In this paper, we follow the standard initialization proposed in [ 21 ] and the combination with the advanced initialization strategies is left for future work.

Optimization. Several optimization approaches for LoRA have been proposed [ 56 , 69 , 26 , 41 ] . For example, Wang et al. [56] aligned the gradient of LoRA with that of full fine-tuning by solving a minimization problem for this gap 2 2 2 We further discuss the relationship between this method and our method in Appendix E . . To fully exploit low-dimensional subspaces spanned by the columns of B B and A A , Zhu et al. [69] regularized those subspaces to capture complementary information. Along this, Li et al. [26] and Park et al. [41] exploited the geometry of Stiefel manifold that imposes the orthogonal constraints on B B and/or A A . On the other hand, exploiting the invariance of LoRA has been studied [ 63 , 50 ] . As explained in Sec. 1 , this approach induces preconditioning at each gradient step described in 4 and achieves efficient optimization compared to the original LoRA. This approach is the first Riemannian preconditioning study for LoRA, and its underlying idea is inspired by the classical low-rank matrix completion problem [ 36 ] . Note that, in the literature on low-rank matrix (or tensor) completion problem, several preconditioning variants have been proposed [ 51 , 65 , 64 ] . Our work follows the Riemannian preconditioning for LoRA proposed in [ 63 , 50 ] but designs a Riemannian metric tailored to LoRA for more efficient optimization.

inspect:2610.20857.question: How were IDEA2PRIOR and the ChatGPT and Gemini Deep Research baselines compared on EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD queries? What was the ground-truth and Hit@5 accounting convention, how were retrieval budgets and evidence access controlled, and what limitations affect the reported advantage?

passages.text: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? This objective is not equivalent to the quality of a general research report. We introduce Idea2Prior, an extension of PaperArena and its implementation [ 1 , 2 ] . The contribution is an engineering and evaluation framework for inspectable idea-to-paper retrieval: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking. This makes it possible to distinguish a discovery miss from a candidate that was retrieved but lost during filtering, or from a task that failed operationally. A high-level result alone cannot make those distinctions.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

2. A retrieval-only execution mode that preserves abstract and PDF evidence assessment while omitting report-specific processing, exposed through local web, Python, CLI, and Notebook interfaces. 3. A three-system historical evaluation with explicit target-recovery, agreement, latency, token, and cost accounting, together with preserved prompts and outputs. 4. Optional implementation-analysis, citation-evolution, planning, benchmark-landscape, and citation-gap extensions, with their earlier exploratory evaluations distinguished from the retrieval benchmark.

Idea2Prior extends PaperArena with an auditable workflow for retrieving and ranking papers from research ideas. Joint ranking combines an abstract-level shortlist with bounded, explicitly partial PDF evidence, while a retrieval-only mode avoids report-specific work. In the documented historical comparison, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3%, exceeding the two browser baselines overall, with a clear HARD-tier exception and longer reported latency. A separate historical cost sample averages $0.0945 per query. These findings motivate focused scholarly retrieval with inspectable evidence; they do not establish general Deep Research superiority, calibrated novelty assessment, or a matched baseline cost advantage.

inspect:2610.19844.question: Find Table 1 and Table 6 for PMRC LLaMA pretraining: exact validation losses at 1.3B and peak GPU memory for PMRC, AdamW, Muon, GaLore, GoLore, Fira, and GUM. Does the paper report measured throughput or wall-clock time for these runs?

passages.text: Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) has demonstrated strong performance in LLM training ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025 ) , while its full-dimensional momentum incurs the same O ⁡ ( m ​ n ) O(mn) optimizer-state memory cost as momentum SGD. At larger model scales, this memory requirement becomes increasingly restrictive and motivates the development of memory-efficient variants of Muon ( Pan et al., 2025a ) . A natural question is whether the momentum of Muon can be maintained in a low-dimensional subspace while preserving the convergence guarantee of full-space Muon . We incorporate the residual correction framework into Muon and develop PMRC, as outlined in Algorithm 3 . Specifically, PMRC projects the stochastic gradient G t G_{t} onto the subspace, maintains the low-rank momentum M t = ( 1 − β ) ​ M t − 1 + β ​ P ⊤ ​ G t ∈ ℝ r × n M_{t}=(1-\beta)M_{t-1}+\beta P^{\top}G_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} and applies the matrix sign to M t M_{t} . Then, PMRC incorporates the orthogonal residual gradient into the parameter update, that is, W t + 1 = W t − η ⁡ ( P ​ msign ⁡ ( M t ) + γ ⁡ ( I − P ​ P ⊤ ) ​ G t ) W_{t+1}=W_{t}-\eta(P\operatorname{msign}(M_{t})+\gamma(I-PP^{\top})G_{t}) , where γ > 0 \gamma>0 controls the residual correction.

We adopt the LLaMA architecture ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) and train models with 60 60 M, 150 150 M, 350 350 M and 1.3 1.3 B parameters. Their architectural configurations are summarized in Table 4 . All models are pretrained on the C4 dataset ( Raffel et al., 2020 ) .

Setup. We train the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models on 2 2 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, the 350 350 M model on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, and the 1.3 1.3 B model on 8 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. The corresponding per-device batch sizes are 256 256 , 256 256 , 160 160 , and 160 160 , yielding global batch sizes of 512 512 , 512 512 , 640 640 , and 1280 1280 , respectively. The sequence length is 512 512 for the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models and 1024 1024 for the 350 350 M and 1.3 1.3 B models. For each model, the number of training steps approximately follows the Chinchilla scaling law ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . For example, the 1.3 1.3 B model is trained for 20480 20480 steps, which corresponds to 20480 × 1024 × 1280 ≈ 26.84 20480\times 1024\times 1280\approx 26.84 billion training tokens, or approximately 20.6 20.6 tokens per parameter. We compare our multi-stage PMRC with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , the AdamW-based GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , GoLore ( He et al., 2025 ) and Fira ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and the Muon-based GUM ( Pan et al., 2025a ) . For projection-based methods, we set the projection rank to r = 256 r=256 and the refresh interval to 100 100 . Since GUM randomly selects a subset of layers for full-rank updates, its memory cost depends on the number of full-rank layers s s . For a fair comparison, we choose s s according to the memory budget of PMRC, setting s = 6 s=6 and r = 128 r=128 for the 60 60 M, 150 150 M, and 350 350 M models, and s = 4 s=4 and r = 128 r=128 for the 1.3 1.3 B model. The peak allocated memory for the 1.3 1.3 B model is reported in Table 6 . The detailed setup, parameter settings and additional pretraining results are deferred to Appendix E.2.2 .

Results. Table 1 presents a comparison of the training and validation losses achieved by PMRC with those achieved by AdamW, Muon, GaLore, GoLore, Fira and GUM. As evidenced by the reported results, PMRC consistently achieves the lowest training and validation losses among memory-efficient methods. The improvement supports the effectiveness of residual correction in practical LLM pretraining. PMRC also requires less optimizer-state memory than AdamW while achieving lower losses at every scale. We further evaluate the pretrained models on seven downstream benchmarks, with complete results reported in Appendix E.2.2 , where PMRC achieves the highest average accuracy among memory-efficient methods.

For all ablations, we pretrain LLaMA-150M on the C4 dataset for 9900 9900 steps with a sequence length of 512 512 and a global batch size of 512 512 . We refresh the projection basis every 100 100 steps and, unless otherwise stated, set the residual cap to ρ = 4 \rho=4 . Effect of the subspace rank. We vary the projection rank over r ∈ { 64,128,256,512 } r\in\{64,128,256,512\} with the residual weight fixed at γ = 8192 \gamma=8192 and all other settings unchanged. Increasing r r expands the subspace in which momentum is maintained and the matrix-sign transformation is applied. As shown in Figure 3 , a larger rank reduces the validation loss, but also increases the memory required to store the projection basis and the projected momentum. For a parameter matrix of size m × n m\times n , this memory cost scales as O ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) O((m+n)r) . These results illustrate the trade-off between validation performance and optimizer-state memory when choosing the subspace rank. Effect of the residual weight. We fix the rank at r = 256 r=256 and vary the residual weight over γ ∈ { 0 , 1024 , 2048 , 4096 , 8192 } \gamma\in\{0,1024,2048,4096,8192\} with all other settings unchanged. Since the residual cap remains active, γ \gamma serves as an upper bound on the effective weight applied to each parameter matrix rather than its exact value. As shown in Figure 4 , the validation loss decreases monotonically as γ \gamma increases over the tested range, with diminishing improvements at larger values. In particular, γ = 0 \gamma=0 removes the residual correction and yields the highest validation loss. This comparison supports the benefit of incorporating gradient information from the orthogonal complement in LLM pretraining. Figure 5: Effect of the residual cap on PMRC.

Effect of the residual cap. We finally examine the role of the residual cap in stabilizing training. Under the practical update in Eq. Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) has demonstrated strong performance in LLM training ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025 ) , while its full-dimensional momentum incurs the same O ⁡ ( m ​ n ) O(mn) optimizer-state memory cost as momentum SGD. At larger model scales, this memory requirement becomes increasingly restrictive and motivates the development of memory-efficient variants of Muon ( Pan et al., 2025a ) . A natural question is whether the momentum of Muon can be maintained in a low-dimensional subspace while preserving the convergence guarantee of full-space Muon . We incorporate the residual correction framework into Muon and develop PMRC, as outlined in Algorithm 3 . Specifically, PMRC projects the stochastic gradient G t G_{t} onto the subspace, maintains the low-rank momentum M t = ( 1 − β ) ​ M t − 1 + β ​ P ⊤ ​ G t ∈ ℝ r × n M_{t}=(1-\beta)M_{t-1}+\beta P^{\top}G_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} and applies the matrix sign to M t M_{t} . Then, PMRC incorporates the orthogonal residual gradient into the parameter update, that is, W t + 1 = W t − η ⁡ ( P ​ msign ⁡ ( M t ) + γ ⁡ ( I − P ​ P ⊤ ) ​ G t ) W_{t+1}=W_{t}-\eta(P\operatorname{msign}(M_{t})+\gamma(I-PP^{\top})G_{t}) , where γ > 0 \gamma>0 controls the residual correction.

We adopt the LLaMA architecture ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) and train models with 60 60 M, 150 150 M, 350 350 M and 1.3 1.3 B parameters. Their architectural configurations are summarized in Table 4 . All models are pretrained on the C4 dataset ( Raffel et al., 2020 ) .

The corresponding per-device batch sizes are 256 256 , 256 256 , 160 160 , and 160 160 , yielding global batch sizes of 512 512 , 512 512 , 640 640 , and 1280 1280 , respectively. The sequence length is 512 512 for the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models and 1024 1024 for the 350 350 M and 1.3 1.3 B models. For each model, the number of training steps approximately follows the Chinchilla scaling law ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . For example, the 1.3 1.3 B model is trained for 20480 20480 steps, which corresponds to 20480 × 1024 × 1280 ≈ 26.84 20480\times 1024\times 1280\approx 26.84 billion training tokens, or approximately 20.6 20.6 tokens per parameter. For projection-based methods, we set the projection rank to r = 256 r=256 and the refresh interval to 100 100 . inspect:2611.08924.question: In the from-scratch QAT and fine-tuning experiments, what model sizes, quantization settings, training budgets, and AdamW, GaLore, and LDAdam baselines were used? Report the measured optimizer-state and peak training memory, throughput, and model-quality results, including settings where ResQAdam does not stay close to AdamW.

passages.text: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top- r r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r × r r\times r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%. Our code is available at https://github.com/LiqunMa/ResQAdam .

Optimization Trajectory and Convergence Alignment. As illustrated in Figure 2 , ResQAdam closely tracks the training-loss trajectory of the dense AdamW baseline. Across all evaluated bit-width configurations and both frameworks, the training loss curves of ResQAdam closely overlap with the baseline from initialization through to the final iterations. The zoomed-in callouts at the end of the training horizons further highlight that ResQAdam maintains stable convergence without divergence. This confirms that our geometry-decoupled and space-specific update strategies sufficiently capture the quantization errors to stabilize the low-bit pretraining process. Curves for the 200M model are in Appendix B . Language Modeling Quality. Table 1 reports the final validation perplexity across model scales and quantization settings. For both QuEST and CAGE, ResQAdam achieves perplexities close to full-state AdamW, with several cases where ResQAdam is slightly better. These results show that ResQAdam largely preserves AdamW-level language modeling quality in from-scratch QAT while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory.

Table 2 compares ResQAdam with AdamW across the three fine-tuning recipes, which differ in data source, training objective and optimization granularity. Across these settings, ResQAdam generally achieves performance close to AdamW in both perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, while reducing optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74%. Although some aggressive W2A16 block-wise settings show larger metric fluctuations, the overall results indicate that ResQAdam can serve as a memory-efficient alternative to AdamW for diverse QAT fine-tuning pipelines.

Table 3: Comparison of optimizer-state memory, total peak memory, and training throughput across different models. Values in each cell are formatted as AdamW / ResQAdam , with relative changes in parentheses. AdamW / ResQAdam Llama 3.2-1B Qwen2.5-1.5B Qwen3 4B-Base Opt. State Memory (GB) 7.78 / 2.16 ( ↓ \downarrow 72.2%) 10.48 / 3.01( ↓ \downarrow 71.3%) 29.07 / 7.78 ( ↓ \downarrow 73.2%) Total Peak Memory (GB) 33.33 / 28.24 ( ↓ \downarrow 15.3%) 43.93 / 37.19 ( ↓ \downarrow 15.3%) 99.14 / 79.77 ( ↓ \downarrow 19.5%) Throughput (# token/s) 29.36k / 28.94k ( ↓ \downarrow 1.4%) 18.31k / 18.19k ( ↓ \downarrow 0.6%) 9.64k / 9.56k ( ↓ \downarrow 0.8%) To evaluate hardware efficiency, we compare ResQAdam against AdamW in terms of optimizer-state memory, total peak memory, and training throughput. Total peak memory is defined as the maximum GPU memory consumed during training, encompassing weights, activations, gradients, and optimizer states. All experiments utilize the Basic QAT framework with a W4A4G128 quantization configuration and a context length of 4096. Training is conducted on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. The micro-batch size is set to 1 with 128 gradient accumulation steps. ResQAdam uses a uniform projection rank of r = 64 r=64 . The reported optimizer-state memory strictly accounts for the transformer backbone and excludes the embedding and language modeling head layers.

As detailed in Table 3 , ResQAdam consistently reduces the optimizer state footprint by over 71% across 3 different LLMs. This efficiency directly translates to a 15.3% to 19.5% reduction in total peak memory. This substantial memory reduction incurs minimal computational overhead. The training throughput decreases by less than 2% compared to standard AdamW in all evaluated cases. These results show that our amortized update strategy substantially alleviates the optimizer-state memory bottleneck of QAT while maintaining competitive training throughput.

Table 4: Perplexity comparison of memory-efficient optimizers under diverse QAT paradigms and quantization configurations. Projection-based optimizers use rank 64. For a fair comparison, all optimizers are tuned with a grid search over learning rates, and the best result is reported. Training Paradigm Q-Cfg ResQAdam GaLore-AdamW GaLore-AdamW8bit LDAdam AdaFactor From-Scratch QAT W2A16G128 20.05 30.61 30.39 28.57 33.01 W4A4G128 18.89 32.93 32.45 28.23 32.84 QAT Fine-Tuning W2A16G128 16.89 19.25 20.32 19.59 27.79 W4A4G128 15.05 15.30 15.64 15.42 14.80 We further compare ResQAdam with two families of memory-efficient optimizers. Low-rank projection methods such as GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) and LDAdam ( Robert et al., 2024 ) restrict adaptive states to a rank- r r subspace obtained from the gradient, with LDAdam adding state transport across changing subspaces and error feedback. Structural factorization methods such as AdaFactor ( Shazeer and Stern, 2018 ) keep the full parameter dimensionality but approximate the second moment by row and column statistics. Table 4 reports the average perplexity on WikiText-2 and C4. In from-scratch QAT, every baseline is far behind ResQAdam in both quantization settings, by a margin much larger than the differences we observe between ResQAdam and AdamW in Table 1 . This is consistent with our hypothesis that confining the update to a low-rank subspace, or replacing the second moment by a factorized approximation, loses part of the correction that QAT relies on. In fine-tuning the picture depends on the bit width. At W2A16G128 the projection-based methods remain clearly behind, whereas at W4A4G128, where quantization error is small, all optimizers land within a narrow range and the choice of optimizer matters little.

We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r × r r\times r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%. Our code is available at https://github.com/LiqunMa/ResQAdam .

Optimization Trajectory and Convergence Alignment. As illustrated in Figure 2 , ResQAdam closely tracks the training-loss trajectory of the dense AdamW baseline. Across all evaluated bit-width configurations and both frameworks, the training loss curves of ResQAdam closely overlap with the baseline from initialization through to the final iterations. The zoomed-in callouts at the end of the training horizons further highlight that ResQAdam maintains stable convergence without divergence. This confirms that our geometry-decoupled and space-specific update strategies sufficiently capture the quantization errors to stabilize the low-bit pretraining process. Curves for the 200M model are in Appendix B . Language Modeling Quality. Table 1 reports the final validation perplexity across model scales and quantization settings. For both QuEST and CAGE, ResQAdam achieves perplexities close to full-state AdamW, with several cases where ResQAdam is slightly better. These results show that ResQAdam largely preserves AdamW-level language modeling quality in from-scratch QAT while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory.

Table 2 compares ResQAdam with AdamW across the three fine-tuning recipes, which differ in data source, training objective and optimization granularity. Across these settings, ResQAdam generally achieves performance close to AdamW in both perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, while reducing optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74%. Although some aggressive W2A16 block-wise settings show larger metric fluctuations, the overall results indicate that ResQAdam can serve as a memory-efficient alternative to AdamW for diverse QAT fine-tuning pipelines.

inspect:2610.23571.question: In Transformer experiments, how does BMuon compare with Muon and other baselines at matched training budget and model quality? Report measured channel-pruning compression, post-pruning quality, training overhead, and whether any low-rank factorization results are reported.

passages.text: NuMuon ( Dolatabadi et al., 2026 ) is the closest prior compression-aware variant of Muon. It imposes a nuclear-norm constraint on Muon’s update direction to improve low-rank compressibility. BMuon instead targets structured compressibility over hidden channels by introducing a global channel budget into Muon’s spectral-norm geometry. Prior work has also incorporated compressibility into training. Lu et al. (2022) train networks for unstructured pruning with Frank–Wolfe under fixed layerwise constraints on the weights, while Zimmer et al. (2025) use Frank–Wolfe under fixed norm constraints for convolutional filter pruning and low-rank compression. BMuon instead leaves the weights unconstrained and modifies Muon’s spectral update geometry for global hidden-channel compression. Resource-constrained structure learning and global structured pruning have been studied across CNNs and Transformers ( Gordon et al., 2018 ; Yu et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; An et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . GRASPrune ( Wang et al., 2026b ) learns gates post hoc on a frozen LLM to select MLP channels and attention KV-head groups under a single global parameter budget, while DABP ( Laroui et al., 2026 ) jointly trains CNN weights and continuous channel gates under a global resource budget. BMuon uses no forward gates; its budget instead controls the channel-wise reweighting of Muon’s spectral update constraint during training.

We first test whether BMuon produces models that can be compressed directly after training without post-compression fine-tuning. We train a small Vision Transformer on CIFAR-100 for 200 epochs over three seeds. We compare Muon, Muon with a proximal Group-Lasso penalty on coupled MLP channels (Muon+GL) ( Yuan and Lin, 2006 ; Wen et al., 2016 ) , NuMuon ( Dolatabadi et al., 2026 ) , and BMuon. NuMuon is particularly relevant as a direct comparison: it modifies the Muon update to improve compressibility, but targets low-rank structure through the singular spectrum, whereas BMuon targets structured MLP-channel compression. BMuon uses α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and a budget annealed to 20 % 20\% of the total MLP-channel mass. Full experimental details in Appendix E.2 .

Figure 2 shows the post-training fragility that motivates this work: Muon falls to 5.72 % 5.72\% test accuracy after only 30 % 30\% MLP-channel pruning. Muon+GL remains robust through 50 % 50\% pruning, while NuMuon degrades more gradually under low-rank compression. Under magnitude-based pruning, BMuon is substantially more compressible than the structured baselines while matching Muon’s dense accuracy: BMuon reaches 71.46 % 71.46\% , versus 71.49 % 71.49\% for Muon, 71.25 % 71.25\% for Muon+GL, and 69.95 % 69.95\% for NuMuon. Using μ \mu for ranking provides a further gain: at 80 % 80\% pruning, BM- μ \mu retains 70.57 % 70.57\% accuracy, compared with 60.84 % 60.84\% for BM-mag, while Muon, Muon+GL, and NuMuon have fallen to 1.93 % 1.93\% , 6.01 % 6.01\% , and 3.84 % 3.84\% , respectively. The advantage of BM-mag under the shared magnitude criterion isolates the compressibility benefit of BMuon training, while the further gain from BM- μ \mu indicates that the learned allocation also carries useful channel-importance information.

Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply under post-training MLP-channel pruning, motivating the question of whether Muon’s spectral geometry can be modified to favor structured compressibility. BMuon addresses this question by reweighting hidden channels within Muon’s spectral-norm constraints and making them compete for a global budget. We show that the resulting norm family recovers Muon and connects it to channel-sparse geometries. In linear two-factor models, Muon admits minimum-cost factorizations with redundant hidden width, whereas under a sufficiently scarce BMuon budget every minimum-cost factorization is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a tractable minorization–maximization approximation to the global allocation oracle. Across vision and language models, BMuon is substantially more robust than Muon to magnitude-based MLP-channel pruning. The learned allocation also provides an effective pruning score and identifies useful non-uniform MLP architectures when retrained from scratch. Several questions remain open. Our theoretical results characterize representation cost in linear two-factor models; studying the implicit bias of BMuon training, particularly beyond the linear setting, is an important direction for future work. Another direction is to design a practical BMuon algorithm with provable approximation guarantees to the oracle. Our experiments focus on MLP hidden channels, and extending the global budget to other structured components of Transformers remains to be explored. Finally, BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments; characterizing this tradeoff at larger model scales is a natural direction for future work.

At evaluation, NuMuon compresses only the 12 MLP weight matrices using truncated SVD; attention weights remain dense. We distribute the retained rank budget as evenly as possible across matrices, with minimum rank 4. At each compression level, we choose the NuMuon rank so that the resulting whole-model parameter count is as close as possible to that of the corresponding structured-pruned model. Table 5 reports the exact post-training compression results corresponding to Fig. 2 . Table 5 : CIFAR-100 post-training compression results. Test accuracy (%) reported as mean ± \pm sample standard deviation over three seeds. All compression levels are evaluated independently from the final epoch-200 checkpoint, without post-compression fine-tuning.
