Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top- r r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r × r r\times r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%. Our code is available at https://github.com/LiqunMa/ResQAdam .

Optimization Trajectory and Convergence Alignment. As illustrated in Figure 2 , ResQAdam closely tracks the training-loss trajectory of the dense AdamW baseline. Across all evaluated bit-width configurations and both frameworks, the training loss curves of ResQAdam closely overlap with the baseline from initialization through to the final iterations. The zoomed-in callouts at the end of the training horizons further highlight that ResQAdam maintains stable convergence without divergence. This confirms that our geometry-decoupled and space-specific update strategies sufficiently capture the quantization errors to stabilize the low-bit pretraining process. Curves for the 200M model are in Appendix B . Language Modeling Quality. Table 1 reports the final validation perplexity across model scales and quantization settings. For both QuEST and CAGE, ResQAdam achieves perplexities close to full-state AdamW, with several cases where ResQAdam is slightly better. These results show that ResQAdam largely preserves AdamW-level language modeling quality in from-scratch QAT while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory.

Table 2 compares ResQAdam with AdamW across the three fine-tuning recipes, which differ in data source, training objective and optimization granularity. Across these settings, ResQAdam generally achieves performance close to AdamW in both perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, while reducing optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74%. Although some aggressive W2A16 block-wise settings show larger metric fluctuations, the overall results indicate that ResQAdam can serve as a memory-efficient alternative to AdamW for diverse QAT fine-tuning pipelines.

passages.text: Setup. We train the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models on 2 2 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, the 350 350 M model on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, and the 1.3 1.3 B model on 8 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. The corresponding per-device batch sizes are 256 256 , 256 256 , 160 160 , and 160 160 , yielding global batch sizes of 512 512 , 512 512 , 640 640 , and 1280 1280 , respectively. The sequence length is 512 512 for the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models and 1024 1024 for the 350 350 M and 1.3 1.3 B models. For each model, the number of training steps approximately follows the Chinchilla scaling law ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . For example, the 1.3 1.3 B model is trained for 20480 20480 steps, which corresponds to 20480 × 1024 × 1280 ≈ 26.84 20480\times 1024\times 1280\approx 26.84 billion training tokens, or approximately 20.6 20.6 tokens per parameter. We compare our multi-stage PMRC with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , the AdamW-based GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , GoLore ( He et al., 2025 ) and Fira ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and the Muon-based GUM ( Pan et al., 2025a ) . For projection-based methods, we set the projection rank to r = 256 r=256 and the refresh interval to 100 100 . Since GUM randomly selects a subset of layers for full-rank updates, its memory cost depends on the number of full-rank layers s s . For a fair comparison, we choose s s according to the memory budget of PMRC, setting s = 6 s=6 and r = 128 r=128 for the 60 60 M, 150 150 M, and 350 350 M models, and s = 4 s=4 and r = 128 r=128 for the 1.3 1.3 B model. The peak allocated memory for the 1.3 1.3 B model is reported in Table 6 . The detailed setup, parameter settings and additional pretraining results are deferred to Appendix E.2.2 .

Results. Table 1 presents a comparison of the training and validation losses achieved by PMRC with those achieved by AdamW, Muon, GaLore, GoLore, Fira and GUM. As evidenced by the reported results, PMRC consistently achieves the lowest training and validation losses among memory-efficient methods. The improvement supports the effectiveness of residual correction in practical LLM pretraining. PMRC also requires less optimizer-state memory than AdamW while achieving lower losses at every scale. We further evaluate the pretrained models on seven downstream benchmarks, with complete results reported in Appendix E.2.2 , where PMRC achieves the highest average accuracy among memory-efficient methods.

2610.23571:f65a409bfb0b235adaaf590032171.question: In Transformer experiments, how does BMuon compare with Muon and other baselines at matched training budget and model quality? Report measured channel-pruning compression, post-pruning quality, training overhead, and whether any low-rank factorization results are reported.

passages.text: NuMuon ( Dolatabadi et al., 2026 ) is the closest prior compression-aware variant of Muon. It imposes a nuclear-norm constraint on Muon’s update direction to improve low-rank compressibility. BMuon instead targets structured compressibility over hidden channels by introducing a global channel budget into Muon’s spectral-norm geometry. Prior work has also incorporated compressibility into training. Lu et al. (2022) train networks for unstructured pruning with Frank–Wolfe under fixed layerwise constraints on the weights, while Zimmer et al. (2025) use Frank–Wolfe under fixed norm constraints for convolutional filter pruning and low-rank compression. BMuon instead leaves the weights unconstrained and modifies Muon’s spectral update geometry for global hidden-channel compression. Resource-constrained structure learning and global structured pruning have been studied across CNNs and Transformers ( Gordon et al., 2018 ; Yu et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; An et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . GRASPrune ( Wang et al., 2026b ) learns gates post hoc on a frozen LLM to select MLP channels and attention KV-head groups under a single global parameter budget, while DABP ( Laroui et al., 2026 ) jointly trains CNN weights and continuous channel gates under a global resource budget. BMuon uses no forward gates; its budget instead controls the channel-wise reweighting of Muon’s spectral update constraint during training.

We first test whether BMuon produces models that can be compressed directly after training without post-compression fine-tuning. We train a small Vision Transformer on CIFAR-100 for 200 epochs over three seeds. We compare Muon, Muon with a proximal Group-Lasso penalty on coupled MLP channels (Muon+GL) ( Yuan and Lin, 2006 ; Wen et al., 2016 ) , NuMuon ( Dolatabadi et al., 2026 ) , and BMuon. NuMuon is particularly relevant as a direct comparison: it modifies the Muon update to improve compressibility, but targets low-rank structure through the singular spectrum, whereas BMuon targets structured MLP-channel compression. passages.text: Figure 3 (a) shows that the singular values are spread across many orders of magnitude, indicating that gradient matrices in the language model setting are very poorly conditioned. This variation does not stem from variation between different matrices: as we can see in Figure 4 (a), the effective rank of the gradient stays below about 280 for most of training. This implies a low-entropy and highly nonuniform distribution within each matrix. Figure 3 (a) also displays the distribution of the gradients after Nesterov momentum is applied. Momentum thins out the low end of the spectrum, suggesting that it suppresses some noisy directions, but otherwise leaves its shape alone and simply shifts scale. This distribution was used to select the absolute thresholds τ \tau for targeted Muon. Averaged over matrices, the top arm lifts about 1% to 28% of the singular directions, and the bottom arm lifts from nearly all of the directions down to about 30%. In terms of squared Frobenius norm, the lifted band holds 32–96% of the momentum in the top arm and at most 13% in the bottom arm. Note that τ \tau is absolute while the bulk of the spectrum sits at different levels in different matrices, so the same τ \tau lifts very different fractions of different matrices. In the top arm this compounds: a matrix whose spectrum falls below τ \tau only gets its raw momentum and effectively stops training, so at the larger thresholds most of the deeper layers are left untouched. Also note that every momentum singular value is far below one, so the targeted region is always amplified, not suppressed.

Validation loss was monitored throughout and remained almost exactly at training loss, so overfitting is not a concern. Every Muon variant drops the loss faster than AdamW over the first hundred steps (Figure 3 (b)), and the lead grows with how much of the spectrum is lifted. Lifting only the top few directions with a high τ \tau already gets much of Muon’s early advantage, but the lead reverses within a few hundred steps, and every top dose ends up behind AdamW with warmup, the smallest ones even behind NSGD (Table 1 ). This is not a matter of step size. Raising the learning rate of the top variants only makes them worse and collapses their rank further (Figure 5 (c)), while Muon at a tenth of its learning rate loses just 0.05. Figure 3 (c,d) plots the final loss against τ \tau and against the fraction of the momentum that is orthogonalized. For both top and bottom targeting, loss falls monotonically with the portion of directions orthogonalized. However, the two arms are not symmetric. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix gets within 0.03 of Muon while orthogonalizing only about 13% of the momentum matrix’s magnitude, while lifting only the top directions remains well short even when they make up 96% of it, and the smallest top doses do worse than lifting nothing. This answers one part of our original question. Despite being a very small portion of the momentum magnitude, the small singular values are not noise. The model can be usefully trained on them, but only once they are amplified to full scale. (a) Gradient effective rank (b) Update effective rank (c) Value matrix effective rank (d) Output matrix effective rank (e) MLP effective rank

Figure 4: Effective rank of the gradient (a) and update (b), averaged over all matrices, and of the value (c), attention-output (d) and MLP (e) parameters, averaged over layers (seed 0). Dashed lines are the warmup variants, the dotted line in (a) marks the start of the learning rate cooldown, and the legend in (b) applies to all panels. We use the effective rank of the gradient and update matrix to help explain our optimizer performances. Since the gradient depends only on the surrounding loss landscape and not the optimizer, it tells us which optimizers enter parts of the loss landscape where many directions are available. This happens quickly for Muon and the targeted variants, while AdamW takes a few hundred steps to get there. During learning rate cooldown, this effective rank grows for every optimizer, because the leading singular values of the gradient shrink while its bulk stays put. In the river-valley picture of Wen et al. (2024) , the component of the gradient along the sharp valley walls dies with the learning rate while the component along the flat floor remains. Gradient rank thus tells us where the iterate sits in the valley, bouncing between the walls or settled on the floor. Meanwhile, the effective rank of the update shows the difference between the different types of targeting, with bottom targeting creating an update shaped like Muon’s, while top targeting creates an even lower rank update than AdamW. (a) Tangent alignment (b) Spectrum-changing update by singular direction (c) Final loss vs. parameter rank

In this paper, we developed a spectrally targeted variant of the Muon optimizer in order to explore why Muon has so much experimental success. By targeting Muon to act on certain singular values either above or below a certain threshold τ , \tau, we were able to do more specific experiments on Muon’s behavior. From our experiments on CIFAR-10, we concluded that Muon’s accuracy improvement requires normalization of all the singular values; by varying τ , \tau, we found that if we normalize singular values, we will measure better evaluation accuracies. However, normalizing only the top singular values yields better tangent alignment and stable weight spectra, hence the primary structural improvements of Muon result from normalizing large singular values, although normalizing smaller ones is important as well.

From our experiments on NanoGPT, we concluded that the small singular values of the momentum are not noise but directions the model can feasibly train on once they are amplified. Orthogonalizing everything but the few largest singular values nearly matches Muon, while orthogonalizing only the top buys an early lead over AdamW and then falls behind even normalized SGD. Keeping the top from dominating the update is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; the tangent alignment shows that the top singular directions are the ones that lie outside the tangent space of the isospectral manifold, so they are what changes the spectrum. This is cheap, however, and is not what drives the loss, as AdamW collapses rank and still performs well. AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, because an elementwise normalized update must build a matrix out of many low rank steps, where an orthogonalized update writes a full-rank matrix in a single step. This explains AdamW’s slower start and why warmup helps it but hurts Muon. Finally, the effective rank of the gradient becomes an effective tool to determine position in the loss landscape, and also shows the difference between optimizers in where the early steps take the parameters.

In future work, we could study the effect on larger transformers to see if our observations scale. Also, since matrices spectra sit at different scale, a threshold relative to the bulk of each spectrum would remove the impact of orthogonalizing a different fraction of directions for each matrix. The radial component of the update also defines an equilibrium weight decay that varies over training and across optimizers, which could be used to create some form of preconditioned weight decay which would prevent change in the spectrum. Given our results, it would also be interesting to consider whether dynamically adapting τ \tau might improve results, as we could normalize either small or large singular values depending on how far along we are in our training.

Orthogonalizing everything but the few largest singular values nearly matches Muon, while orthogonalizing only the top buys an early lead over AdamW and then falls behind even normalized SGD. Keeping the top from dominating the update is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; the tangent alignment shows that the top singular directions are the ones that lie outside the tangent space of the isospectral manifold, so they are what changes the spectrum. This is cheap, however, and is not what drives the loss, as AdamW collapses rank and still performs well. AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, because an elementwise normalized update must build a matrix out of many low rank steps, where an orthogonalized update writes a full-rank matrix in a single step. This explains AdamW’s slower start and why warmup helps it but hurts Muon. Finally, the effective rank of the gradient becomes an effective tool to determine position in the loss landscape, and also shows the difference between optimizers in where the early steps take the parameters.

In future work, we could study the effect on larger transformers to see if our observations scale. Also, since matrices spectra sit at different scale, a threshold relative to the bulk of each spectrum would remove the impact of orthogonalizing a different fraction of directions for each matrix. The radial component of the update also defines an equilibrium weight decay that varies over training and across optimizers, which could be used to create some form of preconditioned weight decay which would prevent change in the spectrum. Given our results, it would also be interesting to consider whether dynamically adapting τ \tau might improve results, as we could normalize either small or large singular values depending on how far along we are in our training.

Figure 3 (a) shows that the singular values are spread across many orders of magnitude, indicating that gradient matrices in the language model setting are very poorly conditioned. This variation does not stem from variation between different matrices: as we can see in Figure 4 (a), the effective rank of the gradient stays below about 280 for most of training. This implies a low-entropy and highly nonuniform distribution within each matrix. Figure 3 (a) also displays the distribution of the gradients after Nesterov momentum is applied. Momentum thins out the low end of the spectrum, suggesting that it suppresses some noisy directions, but otherwise leaves its shape alone and simply shifts scale. This distribution was used to select the absolute thresholds τ \tau for targeted Muon. Averaged over matrices, the top arm lifts about 1% to 28% of the singular directions, and the bottom arm lifts from nearly all of the directions down to about 30%. In terms of squared Frobenius norm, the lifted band holds 32–96% of the momentum in the top arm and at most 13% in the bottom arm. Note that τ \tau is absolute while the bulk of the spectrum sits at different levels in different matrices, so the same τ \tau lifts very different fractions of different matrices. In the top arm this compounds: a matrix whose spectrum falls below τ \tau only gets its raw momentum and effectively stops training, so at the larger thresholds most of the deeper layers are left untouched. Also note that every momentum singular value is far below one, so the targeted region is always amplified, not suppressed.

Validation loss was monitored throughout and remained almost exactly at training loss, so overfitting is not a concern. Every Muon variant drops the loss faster than AdamW over the first hundred steps (Figure 3 (b)), and the lead grows with how much of the spectrum is lifted. Lifting only the top few directions with a high τ \tau already gets much of Muon’s early advantage, but the lead reverses within a few hundred steps, and every top dose ends up behind AdamW with warmup, the smallest ones even behind NSGD (Table 1 ). This is not a matter of step size. Raising the learning rate of the top variants only makes them worse and collapses their rank further (Figure 5 (c)), while Muon at a tenth of its learning rate loses just 0.05. Figure 3 (c,d) plots the final loss against τ \tau and against the fraction of the momentum that is orthogonalized. For both top and bottom targeting, loss falls monotonically with the portion of directions orthogonalized. However, the two arms are not symmetric. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix gets within 0.03 of Muon while orthogonalizing only about 13% of the momentum matrix’s magnitude, while lifting only the top directions remains well short even when they make up 96% of it, and the smallest top doses do worse than lifting nothing. This answers one part of our original question. Despite being a very small portion of the momentum magnitude, the small singular values are not noise. The model can be usefully trained on them, but only once they are amplified to full scale. This happens quickly for Muon and the targeted variants, while AdamW takes a few hundred steps to get there. During learning rate cooldown, this effective rank grows for every optimizer, because the leading singular values of the gradient shrink while its bulk stays put. Gradient rank thus tells us where the iterate sits in the valley, bouncing between the walls or settled on the floor. Meanwhile, the effective rank of the update shows the difference between the different types of targeting, with bottom targeting creating an update shaped like Muon’s, while top targeting creates an even lower rank update than AdamW.
